name: Kitty
summary: A GPU-accelerated terminal emulator that binds PTY-supervised child processes to protocol-driven screen state, session/tab/window composition, input and rendering loops, and configurable remote control.
scope: keyboard, mouse, events, and GPU rendering

features.name: PTY-backed child lifecycle
features.description: kitty creates and supervises shell child processes through PTYs, with process groups, signal handling, exit tracking, and nonblocking I/O forming the boundary between terminal state and the operating system.
benefits: Provides conventional shell compatibility through a real PTY
Makes child exit and signal transitions observable to the terminal window
costs: PTY behavior, process groups, and platform signal semantics vary by host
Each child adds kernel process and buffer resources

features.name: Screen state and terminal protocol interpreter
features.description: kitty maintains screen buffers, cursor and mode state, and applies terminal control sequences to mutate cells, scrollback, selection, and rendering-relevant state.
benefits: Separates byte-stream interpretation from window drawing
Supports rich terminal protocols and persistent scrollback state
costs: Large scrollback and graphics state consume memory
Protocol compatibility and state transitions are complex

features.name: Session, tab, and window composition
features.description: kitty composes OS windows from tabs and terminal windows, with session definitions and layout policies controlling shell placement and restoration.
benefits: Provides reusable multi-window layouts and session restoration
Keeps shell processes associated with explicit terminal windows
costs: Layout and process restoration can create lifecycle coupling
More panes increase input focus and resource-management complexity

features.name: Event, input, and GPU rendering boundary
features.description: kitty separates child I/O from the main loop through ChildMonitor's I/O thread, per-screen buffers, wakeups, and parsing callbacks. Window handling routes input and selection actions while the shader implementation manages GPU textures and drawing. Child-output readiness and frame scheduling must coordinate without treating every PTY read as a separate frame.
benefits: Integrates input dispatch, damage/redraw, and terminal output in one interactive loop
Supports GPU-accelerated text and image rendering
costs: Backend and compositor behavior remains platform-specific
Rendering and input responsiveness compete with child-output volume

features.name: Remote-control command authority
features.description: kitty remote control can inspect windows, inject text, and create or close windows. It is disabled by default; password mode authorizes TTY/socket requests, while socket-only accepts socket requests and denies TTY requests. Clipboard policy is separate: writes are allowed and reads require confirmation by default, with a configurable maximum buffered clipboard size.
benefits: Allows automation without embedding application logic in every shell
costs: A reachable control endpoint can affect processes, input, or displayed data
Security depends on transport and permission configuration

mathematical_views.question: How does child output transition through PTY reads, escape-sequence parsing, screen state, and redraw?
assumptions: PTY reads produce ordered byte streams
Rendering observes screen state after event-loop scheduling

mathematical_views.question: How do OS windows, tabs, terminal windows, child processes, and layouts compose and terminate?
assumptions: Tabs and windows are explicit containment nodes
A terminal window owns or supervises a child process
Layout restoration is a configuration relation, not proof of process persistence

mathematical_views.question: Which remote-control operations can reach which session and process resources?
assumptions: Permission and transport policy determine authority edges
Reachability does not prove a command is safe
